items.title: Focus Question: How do the particles in a solid differ from those in a fluid, and what does this say about shape and volume?

answer.html: In a solid the particles are held in fixed positions (vibrating in place) by strong cohesive forces, so a solid keeps a definite shape and volume. In a fluid the particles slide past one another, so a fluid flows and takes the shape of its container.

items.title: Get It? Does a block of solid paraffin wax sink or float in melted paraffin? What does this tell you about the densities of the solid and liquid?

answer.html: The solid wax sinks, so it is denser than the melted wax, as for most substances: the particles fit more closely together in the solid. (Water is the main exception, since ice floats.)

items.title: Get It? Give one example of a product that depends on malleability and one that depends on ductility.

answer.html: Malleability: copper sheet used for roofing (metal hammered or rolled into sheets). Ductility: steel cable or aluminum wire (metal drawn into wire).

items.title: Figure 20, Infer: What could happen to steel railroad rails laid end to end with no gaps between them on a very hot day?

answer.html: The rails would expand with nowhere to go. They would push against one another and buckle or bend sideways out of line.

items.title: Practice Problem 39: A copper roof panel is 4.88 m long at -18°C. How much longer is it on a hot day when its temperature reaches 41°C? The coefficient of linear expansion for copper is 17 × 10−6 °C−1.

body.html: 𝐿<sub>1</sub> = 4.88 m, 𝑇<sub>1</sub> = −18°C, 𝑇<sub>2</sub> = 41°C, 𝛼<sub>Cu</sub> = 17 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>6</sup> °C<sup>−</sup><sup>1</sup>. Find 𝛥𝐿.
𝛥𝐿= 𝛼𝐿<sub>1</sub>𝛥𝑇.

answer.html: 4.9 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>3</sup> m (4.9 mm) longer

check.html: A few millimeters over a few meters for a 59°C swing is typical.

items.title: Practice Problem 40: A brass piece is 14.2 cm long at 21°C. It is heated in a furnace to 830°C. What is its length at 830°C? Use 𝛼brass = 19 × 10−6 °C−1.

body.html: 𝐿<sub>1</sub> = 14.2 cm, 𝑇<sub>1</sub> = 21°C, 𝑇<sub>2</sub> = 830°C, 𝛼<sub>brass</sub> = 19 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>6</sup> °C<sup>−</sup><sup>1</sup>. Find 𝐿<sub>2</sub>.
𝐿<sub>2</sub> = 𝐿<sub>1</sub> + 𝛼𝐿<sub>1</sub>𝛥𝑇.

check.html: The piece grows by about 1.5%, reasonable for a temperature change of about 800°C.

items.title: Practice Problem 41: A glass beaker holds 250 mL of ethanol at 5.0°C. The beaker and ethanol are warmed to 28.0°C. Given 𝛽ethanol = 1100 × 10−6 °C−1 and 𝛽glass = 27 × 10−6 °C−1, how much ethanol spills over the rim if the beaker was filled to the brim?

body.html: 𝑉<sub>1</sub> = 250 mL, 𝑇<sub>1</sub> = 5.0°C, 𝑇<sub>2</sub> = 28.0°C; 𝛽<sub>ethanol</sub> = 1100 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>6</sup> °C<sup>−</sup><sup>1</sup>, 𝛽<sub>glass</sub> = 27 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>6</sup> °C<sup>−</sup><sup>1</sup>. Find the volume that spills.
Both the ethanol and the beaker expand. 𝛥𝑉= 𝛽𝑉<sub>1</sub>𝛥𝑇. The ethanol spills by the amount that the liquid expands more than the beaker's capacity.
𝑉<sup>spill</sup> = (𝛽<sub>ethanol</sub> −𝛽<sub>glass</sub>)𝑉<sup>1</sup>𝛥𝑇= (1100 −27) × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>6</sup> °C<sup>−</sup><sup>1</sup>(250 mL)(23.0°C) = 6.2 mL

answer.html: About 6.2 mL spills

check.html: The ethanol alone would expand by about 6.3 mL, and the glass offsets a little of that.

items.title: Practice Problem 42: A tanker truck is loaded with 36,480 L of heating oil at 4.0°C and delivers it on a day when the oil has warmed to 35.0°C. The coefficient of volume expansion of the oil is 900 × 10−6 °C−1. (a) What volume does the oil occupy at 35.0°C? (b) If the tank had been filled to the brim at 4.0°C, what would have happened?

body.html: 𝑉<sub>1</sub> = 36, 480 L at 𝑇<sub>1</sub> = 4.0°C; 𝑇<sub>2</sub> = 35.0°C; 𝛽<sub>oil</sub> = 900 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>6</sup> °C<sup>−</sup><sup>1</sup>. Find (a) the volume at 𝑇<sup>2</sup>, (b) what happens to a brimful tank.
A liquid expands when heated by 𝛥𝑉= 𝛽𝑉<sub>1</sub>𝛥𝑇. Ignore the (much smaller) expansion of the tank. Work (a):

answer.html: (a) About 3.750 × 10<sup>4</sup> L (about 1020 L more than was loaded). (b) The oil expanded as it warmed, so a tank filled to the brim would overflow by about 1020 L (the same mass now occupies a larger volume, so it is less dense).

check.html: A rise of 31°C times 0.090% per °C is about 2.8%, and 2.8% of 36,480 is about 1020 L.

items.title: Practice Problem 43: A copper rod 1.20 cm in diameter fits through a hole in a steel plate at 28.0°C. Both are cooled to -12.0°C. Find how much smaller the rod's diameter becomes relative to the hole's diameter. Use 𝛼Cu = 17 × 10−6 and 𝛼steel = 12 × 10−6 °C−1. (Assume the rod and hole start at the same diameter.)

body.html: 𝑑= 1.20 cm at 28.0°C; cooled to −12.0°C (𝛥𝑇= −40.0°C); 𝛼<sub>Cu</sub> = 17 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>6</sup>, 𝛼<sub>steel</sub> = 12 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>6</sup> °C<sup>−</sup><sup>1</sup>.
The hole in the steel shrinks as though it were a steel disc, and the copper rod shrinks more because its 𝛼 is larger. The difference in diameters is the gap.

answer.html: The rod's diameter is 2.4 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>4</sup> cm (2.4 𝜇m) smaller than the hole's, so the spacing on each side is about 1.2 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>4</sup> cm.

check.html: A few micrometers is tiny but is what the difference in 𝛼 gives: (5 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>6</sup>)(1.20)(40).

items.title: Practice Problem 44 (Challenge): An aluminum ruler is correct at 20.0°C. By what percentage is its length wrong at 48.0°C, and does it read too high or too low? Use 𝛼Al = 23 × 10−6 °C−1.

body.html: Correct at 20.0°C; 𝑇<sub>2</sub> = 48.0°C, so 𝛥𝑇= 28.0°C; 𝛼= 23 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>6</sup> °C<sup>−</sup><sup>1</sup>. Find the percentage error.
Fractional change in length is 𝛥𝐿/ 𝐿<sub>1</sub> = 𝛼𝛥𝑇.

answer.html: The ruler is about 0.064% too long, so each marked centimeter is slightly too large and every reading would be 0.064% too low

check.html: This is under 1 mm per meter, a small but measurable error. A longer ruler spans more length per mark, so it reads less than the true length.

items.title: Physics Challenge: A 2.00-m bar must expand like a 2.00-m brass bar ( 𝛼brass = 19 × 10−6 °C−1). It is made by joining a steel section (𝛼steel = 12 × 10−6) and an aluminum section (𝛼Al = 23 × 10−6). Find the length of each section.

body.html: Total length 2.00 m, made of steel and aluminum, and it must expand like a 2.00-m brass bar. Find 𝐿<sub>steel</sub> and 𝐿<sub>Al</sub>.
For the same 𝛥𝑇, the total expansion must be equal: 𝛼<sub>steel</sub>𝐿<sub>steel</sub> + 𝛼<sub>Al</sub>𝐿<sub>Al</sub> = 𝛼<sub>brass</sub>(2.00 m), with 𝐿<sub>steel</sub> + 𝐿<sub>Al</sub> = 2.00 m.
Substitute 𝐿<sub>steel</sub> = 2.00 −𝐿<sub>Al</sub>:
𝐿<sub>Al</sub> = (2.00 m)𝛼<sup>brass</sup> −𝛼<sup>steel</sup>

answer.html: Steel section 0.73 m and aluminum section 1.27 m

check.html: The brass coefficient lies between those of steel and aluminum, so both are needed, with more of the aluminum because 19 is closer to 23 than to 12.

items.title: Check Your Progress 45: You must install a 1.20-m-wide steel panel in an aluminum frame. Aluminum changes size about twice as fast as steel (23 × 10−6 compared with 12 × 10−6 °C−1). If the installation is done on a hot day and the temperature may later drop by 45°C, should the fit be snug or loose? How much extra clearance is needed?

body.html: In the cold, the aluminum frame opening shrinks more than the steel panel, so the clearance decreases. If there is no extra room, the panel would be squeezed.
The change in clearance is (23 −12) × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>6</sup>(1.20 m)(45) = 5.9 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>4</sup> m, about 0.59 mm.

answer.html: Leave the fit loose, with at least about 0.6 mm of extra room on the hot day. When it cools, the aluminum frame shrinks about 0.6 mm more than the steel panel.

items.title: Check Your Progress 46: Is table salt a crystalline or amorphous solid? Is window glass? Explain the difference.

answer.html: Table salt is a crystalline solid, with its particles in a regular repeating lattice. Window glass is an amorphous solid, which has a definite shape and volume but no regular crystal structure.

items.title: Check Your Progress 47: Could you triple the length of an aluminum rod by heating it? ( 𝛼Al = 23 × 10−6 °C−1; aluminum melts at about 660°C.)

body.html: Tripling means 𝛥𝐿= 2𝐿<sub>1</sub>, so 𝛥𝑇= 2 / 𝛼.

answer.html: No. It would require a temperature rise of about 87, 000°C, but aluminum melts at about 660°C long before that.

items.title: Check Your Progress 48: A table lists these materials: aluminum (𝛼= 23 × 10−6, no 𝛽 given), mercury (𝛼 listed as "not applicable", 𝛽= 180 × 10−6), brass (𝛼= 19 × 10−6, no 𝛽 given) and glycerin (𝛼 "not applicable", 𝛽= 500 × 10−6). Can the table be used to tell solids from liquids?

answer.html: Yes. Aluminum and brass have a coefficient of linear expansion 𝛼, because solids keep a fixed shape and their length changes make sense. Mercury and glycerin have only a coefficient of volume expansion, since a liquid has no definite shape or length. So the solids are aluminum and brass, and the liquids are mercury and glycerin.

items.title: Check Your Progress 49: Why does a thin steel strip spring back after a small bend, while a strip of clay stays bent?

body.html: Particles in a solid are bonded by attractive forces (like springs) at fixed positions.

Bending the steel shifts the particles slightly, and the bonds provide a restoring force that pulls them back, as long as the elastic limit is not exceeded. In clay the particles slide past one another more easily, so there is little restoring force, and it keeps the new shape.

answer.html: The steel springs back because the bonds between its particles act like springs that pull the particles back to their original positions. Clay's particles slide to new positions, so it stays bent.

items.title: Check Your Progress 50: Critical thinking. A brass washer is heated. Does the diameter of the hole in its center get larger, get smaller or stay the same?

body.html: Thermal expansion scales every dimension of the material, including the hole (as if the whole washer were enlarged like a photo).
Every part of the washer, including the diameter of the hole, becomes larger by the same fraction.

answer.html: The hole gets larger.

items.title: 3D Thinking: Communicate Scientific Ideas (write a blog post about a different example of a multiple discovery)

body.html: A multiple discovery is a discovery made independently by two or more people or groups at about the same time.

Example: the planet Neptune, whose position was calculated independently by John Couch Adams and Urbain Le Verrier in 1845 and 1846, and then found by telescope in 1846. Another example is non-Euclidean geometry (Bolyai and Lobachevsky). A blog post outline: (1) the discovery, (2) who found it and when, (3) why independent work happened (the same data and mathematics were available to both), (4) why independent confirmation strengthens scientific evidence.

answer.html: Adams and Le Verrier each predicted the position of Neptune from irregularities in the orbit of Uranus. Reaching the same answer by separate calculations made the prediction much more convincing, just as two independent supersolid teams support one another.

items.title: Revisit the Phenomenon and CER: How will the blue dye solution move through the branching network of channels in the plastic chip?

body.html: Summarize the evidence from each lesson and test the claim made at the start.

Evidence: (Lesson 1) liquids flow and take the shape of the channels. (Lesson 2) Adhesive forces larger than cohesive forces draw the liquid along the narrow channels by capillary action, and viscosity slows it. (Lesson 3) Pressure is transmitted through the liquid, and the liquid speeds up (with lower pressure) in narrower channels. (Lesson 4) The solid plastic walls keep their shape and do not deform under the liquid.

answer.html: The evidence supports the opening claim: the dye solution is drawn into the channels by capillary action and splits at each branch, moving smoothly and slowly in the fine channels because of viscosity. If a student's original claim differed (for example, that only gravity pulls the liquid), it should be revised to include capillary action.

items.title: Data Analysis Lab, Sinking or floating? (Problems 1 and 2): Five blocks A to E have the densities below, and water has a density of 1.00 g/cm³. Six possible positions in a tank of water are shown in the figure. (1) Choose a position for each block. (2) Explain your choices.

question.html: Block Density (g/cm³) A 0.70 Block Density (g/cm³) B 0.92 C 1.00 D 1.15 E 1.30

body.html: Densities as in the table; water is 1.00 g/cm<sup>3</sup>. From the figure: position 1 floats with about 30% of the block above the surface; position 2 floats with about 8% above; position 3 floats with about 70% above; position 4 hangs at middle depth; position 5 floats with about 50% above; position 6 is on the bottom.

An object floats if its density is below water's, with the submerged fraction equal to 𝜌<sub>object</sub> / 𝜌<sub>water</sub>. An object with exactly water's density is neutrally buoyant and can hang at any depth. An object denser than water sinks to the bottom.
Fraction above the surface = 1 −𝜌/ 𝜌<sub>water</sub>:
Block C has the same density as water, so it hangs in the water. Blocks D and E are denser than water and sink to the bottom.

answer.html: A: position 1 (about 30% above water). B: position 2 (about 8% above). C: position 4 (neutrally buoyant, hanging at mid-depth). D and E: position 6 (they sink to the bottom). Positions 3 and 5 are not used.

Floating objects have a density less than water's ( 1.00 g/cm<sup>3</sup>): A (0.70) and B (0.92). The less dense A sits higher, with more above the surface (30%) than B (8%). Position 3 (about 70% above) would need a density near 0.30 g/cm³, and position 5 (about 50% above) one near 0.50 g/cm³; no block has either. Block C has exactly the density of water, so the buoyant force equals its weight at any depth and it can hang at mid-depth (position 4). Blocks D (1.15) and E (1.30) are denser than water, so the buoyant force is less than their weight and they sink to the bottom (position 6).

items.title: Focus Question: How are solids different from fluids?

answer.html: A solid keeps a definite shape and volume because its particles are held in fixed positions (vibrating in place) by strong cohesive forces. Fluids flow because their particles can move past each other.

items.title: Get It? For most substances, how do the densities of the solid and liquid compare?

answer.html: The solid is denser than the liquid, because the particles fit more closely in the solid. (Water is the main exception.)

items.title: Get It? Malleability and ductility examples

answer.html: Malleability: gold leaf or aluminum foil (metal sheets). Ductility: copper wire (electrical wiring).

answer.html: The road's concrete would expand with nowhere to go. It would push against its neighbors and buckle, crack or break up.

items.title: Practice Problem 39: Aluminum siding

body.html: 𝐿<sub>1</sub> = 3.66 m, 𝑇<sub>1</sub> = −28°C, 𝑇<sub>2</sub> = 39°C (from Figure 22), 𝛼<sub>Al</sub> = 23 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>6</sup> °C<sup>−</sup><sup>1</sup>. Find 𝛥𝐿.

items.title: Practice Problem 41: Glass beaker of water

body.html: 𝑉<sub>1</sub> = 400 mL, 𝑇<sub>1</sub> = 4.4°C, 𝑇<sub>2</sub> = 30.0°C; 𝛽<sub>water</sub> = 210 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>6</sup> °C<sup>−</sup><sup>1</sup>, 𝛽<sub>glass</sub><sub> </sub><sub>(soft)</sub> = 27 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>6</sup> °C<sup>−</sup><sup>1</sup> (Table 2). Find the volume that spills.
Both the water and the beaker expand. 𝛥𝑉= 𝛽𝑉<sub>1</sub>𝛥𝑇. The water spills by the amount the water expands more than the beaker's capacity.
𝑉<sup>spill</sup> = (𝛽<sub>water</sub> −𝛽<sub>glass</sub>)𝑉<sup>1</sup>𝛥𝑇= (210 −27) × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>6</sup> °C<sup>−</sup><sup>1</sup>(400 mL)(25.6°C) = 1.9 mL

answer.html: About 1.9 mL spills

check.html: The water alone would expand by 2.2 mL, and the glass offsets a little of that.

items.title: Practice Problem 42: Tank truck of gasoline

body.html: 𝑉<sub>1</sub> = 45, 725 L at 𝑇<sub>1</sub> = 28.0°C; 𝑇<sub>2</sub> = −12.0°C; 𝛽<sub>gasoline</sub> = 950 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>6</sup> °C<sup>−</sup><sup>1</sup>. Find (a) the volume delivered, (b) what happened.

answer.html: (a) About 4.399 × 10<sup>4</sup> L is delivered (about 1740 L less than was loaded). (b) The gasoline contracted as it cooled; the same mass occupies a smaller volume (it became denser), so none was lost.

check.html: A fall of 40°C times 0.095% per °C is about 3.8%, and 3.8% of 45,725 is about 1740 L.

items.title: Practice Problem 43: Aluminum rod in a steel plate

body.html: 𝑑= 0.85 cm at 30.0°C; cooled to 0.0°C (𝛥𝑇= −30.0°C); 𝛼<sub>Al</sub> = 23 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>6</sup>, 𝛼<sub>steel</sub> = 12 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>6</sup> °C<sup>−</sup><sup>1</sup>.
The hole in the steel shrinks as though it were a steel disc, and the aluminum rod shrinks more, since its 𝛼 is larger. The difference in diameters is the gap.

check.html: A few micrometers is tiny but is what the difference in 𝛼 gives: (11 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>6</sup>)(0.85)(30).

items.title: Practice Problem 44 (Challenge): Steel ruler at -30.0°C

body.html: Correct at 30.0°C; 𝑇<sub>2</sub> = −30.0°C, so 𝛥𝑇= −60.0°C; 𝛼= 12 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>6</sup> °C<sup>−</sup><sup>1</sup>. Find the percentage error.
Fractional change in length is 𝛥𝐿/ 𝐿<sub>1</sub> = 𝛼𝛥𝑇.

answer.html: The ruler is about 0.072% too short, so every reading would be 0.072% too large

items.title: Physics Challenge: A bar that expands like copper

body.html: Total length 1.00 m, made of iron (𝛼<sub>Fe</sub> = 12 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>6</sup>) and aluminum (𝛼<sub>Al</sub> = 23 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>6</sup>), and it must expand like a 1.00-m copper bar ( 𝛼<sub>Cu</sub> = 17 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>6</sup> °C<sup>−</sup><sup>1</sup>). Find 𝐿<sub>Fe</sub> and 𝐿<sub>Al</sub>.

Substitute 𝐿<sub>Fe</sub> = 1.00 −𝐿<sub>Al</sub>:

answer.html: Iron bar 0.55 m and aluminum bar 0.45 m

items.title: Check Your Progress 45: Installing an aluminum screen door in a concrete frame

body.html: Aluminum (𝛼= 23 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>6</sup>) changes size about twice as fast as concrete (12 × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>6</sup> ). In the cold, the door shrinks more than the frame, so the gap grows.
For a 1-m door and a 60°C temperature drop, the gap grows by (23 −12) × 10<sup>−</sup><sup>6</sup>(1.0 m)(60) = 0.66 mm.

answer.html: Make it fit tightly (very little extra room) on the hot day. In winter the door contracts more than the concrete, so the gap widens by about a millimeter per meter of door.

items.title: Check Your Progress 46: Candle wax vs ice

answer.html: Ice is a crystalline solid, with its molecules in a regular repeating lattice. Candle wax is an amorphous solid, which has no regular crystal structure (though it has a definite shape and volume).

items.title: Check Your Progress 47: Heating copper to double its length

body.html: Doubling means 𝛥𝐿= 𝐿<sub>1</sub>, so 𝛥𝑇= 1 / 𝛼.

answer.html: No. It would require a temperature rise of about 59, 000°C, but copper melts at about 1085°C long before that.

items.title: Check Your Progress 48: Does Table 2 distinguish solids from liquids?

answer.html: Yes. Solids have a coefficient of linear expansion 𝛼 (they keep a fixed shape, so length changes make sense), while the liquids listed have only a coefficient of volume expansion (their 𝛼 is "not applicable", since they have no definite shape or length).

items.title: Check Your Progress 49: Bending and binding in solids

body.html: Particles in a solid are bonded by attractive forces (like springs) at fixed positions.

Bending moves the particles slightly out of position, and the bonds provide a restoring force, so the solid resists bending and springs back if the elastic limit is not exceeded. In a liquid the particles slide past one another, so there are no fixed positions to restore.

answer.html: A solid resists bending because its particles are held in place by bonds that act like springs and pull them back. In a liquid the particles are free to slide past one another, so there is no restoring force on its shape.

items.title: Check Your Progress 50: Critical thinking, heated iron ring with a gap

body.html: Thermal expansion scales every dimension of the material, including the gap (as if the whole ring were enlarged like a photo).
Every part of the ring, including the width of the gap, becomes larger by the same fraction.

answer.html: The gap becomes wider.

items.title: 3D Thinking: Communicate Scientific Ideas (multiple discovery blog post)

body.html: A multiple discovery is a discovery made independently by two or more people or groups at about the same time.

Example: the theory of evolution by natural selection, published by Charles Darwin and Alfred Russel Wallace in 1858. Other examples include calculus (Newton and Leibniz), oxygen (Scheele and Priestley), and the telephone (Bell and Gray). A blog post outline: (1) the discovery, (2) who found it and when, (3) why independent work happened (shared knowledge and tools), (4) why independent confirmation strengthens scientific evidence.

answer.html: Darwin and Wallace independently proposed natural selection in 1858, an example of multiple discovery that, like the two supersolid teams, supports the idea because the same conclusion was reached by separate paths.

items.title: Revisit the Phenomenon and CER: How will the fluid flow through the device?

body.html: Summarize the evidence from each lesson and test the claim made at the start.

Evidence: (Lesson 1) liquids flow and take the shape of the grooves. (Lesson 2) Adhesive forces larger than cohesive forces draw the liquid along the narrow grooves by capillary action, and viscosity slows it. (Lesson 3) Pressure is transmitted through the fluid, and the fluid speeds up (with lower pressure) in narrower channels. (Lesson 4) The solid walls are not deformed by the liquid and keep the channel shape.

answer.html: The evidence supports the opening claim: the liquid is drawn into the grooves by capillary action and splits at each branch, flowing smoothly and slowly in the fine channels because of viscosity. If the student's original claim differed (for example, that gravity alone drives the flow), it should be revised to include capillary action.

items.title: Data Analysis Lab, Sinking or floating? (Problems 1 and 2)

body.html: Densities (g/cm³): A 0.85, B 0.95, C 1.05, D 1.15, E 1.25. Water is 1.00 g/cm<sup>3</sup>. I read the figure for the six positions: position 1 floats with about 40% of the block above the surface; position 2 floats with about 10% above; position 3 has its top level with the surface (fully submerged, barely); positions 4 and 5 are fully submerged and suspended at middle depths; position 6 is on the bottom.

An object floats if its density is below water's, with the submerged fraction equal to 𝜌<sub>object</sub> / 𝜌<sub>water</sub>. An object denser than water sinks to the bottom, because a free object cannot hover at a middle depth unless its density equals water's exactly.
Fraction above the surface = 1 −𝜌/ 𝜌<sub>water</sub>:
Objects C, D and E have density greater than water's and sink all the way down.

answer.html: A: position 2 (about 15% above water, closest to the 10% shown). B: position 3 (only about 5% above, so it floats with its top nearly level with the surface). C, D and E: position 6 (they sink to the bottom). Positions 1, 4 and 5 are not used.

Floating objects have a density less than water's ( 1.00 g/cm<sup>3</sup>): A (0.85) and B (0.95). The less dense A sits higher, with more above the surface (15%) than B (5%). Position 1 (about 40% above) would need a density near 0.60 g/cm³, which no object has. Objects C, D and E have densities above water's, so the buoyant force is less than the weight and they sink to the bottom (position 6). Positions 4 and 5 would need an object with the same density as water (neutral buoyancy), and none is listed. B could instead be placed at position 2 if a 5% to 10% difference in the picture is counted as close enough; the reasoning on densities remains the same.
